t: Convex Polygon — Cross Product Sign Consistency
o: We must decide whether a simple polygon, given as an ordered list of vertices, is convex. A polygon is convex exactly when every interior angle is at most 180°, i.e., when walking along the boundary you always turn the same way (all left turns or all right turns). In Example 1 the square [[0,0],[0,5],[5,5],[5,0]] makes only left (counterclockwise) turns, so it is convex. In Example 2, visiting [10,0] then [5,5] then back toward earlier points creates a turn in the opposite direction (a reflex vertex), so it is not convex. Constraints allow up to 10^4 points, so any O(n) or O(n log n) geometric test is fine; the key is avoiding floating-point angles and using exact integer arithmetic.
k: A polygon is convex iff every consecutive triple of vertices turns in the same direction.
The direction of a turn at point B between A and C is given by the sign of the 2D cross product (B-A) x (C-B).
Collinear triples (cross product zero) are allowed; just skip them instead of failing.
Integer coordinates keep cross products exact — no floating point needed.

a.i: For each triple of consecutive vertices (prev, cur, next) compute the z-component of the cross product of vectors prev->cur and cur->next: dx1*dy2 - dy1*dx2. If all nonzero values share one sign, every turn goes the same way and the polygon is convex; if we see both positive and negative values, there is a reflex vertex. Zero means collinear points, which is fine for convexity, so we simply ignore them. This handles both clockwise and counterclockwise input orderings automatically.
s: Let n = len(points). Iterate i from 0 to n-1 with prev = points[(i-1+n)%n], cur = points[i], next = points[(i+1)%n].
Compute cross = (cur.x - prev.x)*(next.y - cur.y) - (cur.y - prev.y)*(next.x - cur.x).
If cross < 0 record that we saw a negative turn; if cross > 0 record a positive turn.
After the loop return true iff we never saw both signs (positiveSeen and negativeSeen cannot both be true).
a.t: O(n) — one pass over all vertices computing a constant-time cross product per triple.
a.sp: O(1) — only two boolean flags and loop variables.

a.i: For a convex polygon, the sum of exterior turning angles over a full traversal is exactly ±360°. Compute the signed turning angle at each vertex using atan2 on the incoming and outgoing edge directions and sum them. If the total magnitude is close to 360°, the polygon is convex. This works but relies on floating point and trigonometry, making it slower and error-prone compared to the exact integer cross-product method.
s: For each vertex compute incoming vector v1 = cur - prev and outgoing vector v2 = next - cur.
Compute the signed turn angle via atan2(cross(v1,v2), dot(v1,v2)).
Sum all angles around the polygon.
Return true if |sum| is within epsilon of 2π, otherwise false.

c.python:
import math

class Solution:
    def isConvex(self, points: List[List[int]]) -> bool:
        n = len(points)
        total = 0.0
        for i in range(n):
            px, py = points[i - 1]
            cx, cy = points[i]
            nx, ny = points[(i + 1) % n]
            v1 = (cx - px, cy - py)
            v2 = (nx - cx, ny - cy)
            ang = math.atan2(v1[0] * v2[1] - v1[1] * v2[0],
                             v1[0] * v2[0] + v1[1] * v2[1])
            total += ang
        return abs(abs(total) - 2 * math.pi) < 1e-9

a.t: O(n) — one pass, but each step uses trigonometric functions with larger constants than Approach 1.

w: In an interview, lead with the cross-product approach: it is O(n), exact with integer arithmetic, and handles both orientations naturally. Pitfalls to watch: forgetting that collinear triples (cross = 0) are legal and should be skipped rather than rejected; using floats where integer cross products suffice; and mishandling wrap-around indices at the ends of the array (use modular indexing). Edge cases include triangles (always convex if simple), polygons with three or more collinear consecutive points, and clockwise vs counterclockwise ordering. Likely follow-ups: detect whether the polygon is oriented clockwise or counterclockwise (sum the signed areas), handle duplicate/collinear points explicitly, or extend to checking strict convexity where no three points may be collinear.
